summary.title: Limitations of Flat File Data Storage
summary.summary: The team discussed the operational challenges and inherent inefficiencies of using flat files for data storage compared to full database management systems.
key_concepts: Difficulty in performing efficient record lookups (search performance).
Lack of scalability when sharing data across multiple applications or distributed systems.
Concurrency issues such as race conditions when multiple threads attempt simultaneous writes.
Motivation for moving from ad-hoc file management to structured database systems.

summary.title: Limitations of Flat Files for Database Reliability
summary.summary: The presentation presented two fundamental challenges that arise when using simple flat files for data storage: maintaining atomic durability during system crashes and supporting data replication for high availability.
key_concepts: Durability issues during incomplete record updates due to system crashes.
The challenge of replicating flat-file data across multiple nodes to ensure high availability.
Motivating the need for more complex database management systems beyond simple flat files.

summary.summary: The group discussed how applications interact with external schemas (views), which are insulated from the underlying logical and physical schemas, allowing the DBMS to optimize storage and data representation without affecting application logic. Data independence isolates application logic from low-level physical data storage details. The DBMS manages and re-optimizes the database layout dynamically based on environmental changes, workload, data usage.

summary.title: Data Manipulation Languages (DML)
summary.summary: The slide defines Data Manipulation Languages as the interface through which applications interact with a Database Management System, and categorizes them into two fundamental types based on query execution logic.
key_concepts: DMLs function as the API between applications and a DBMS for data storage and retrieval.

Non-procedural (Declarative) DMLs focus only on defining the desired end result rather than the retrieval process.
